Hooey means nonsense — words, ideas, claims, or beliefs that are completely false, foolish, or without any real basis in truth or fact. When you call something hooey, you are saying it is so stupid, baseless, or untrue that it is not even worth taking seriously.

Think of it this way: if someone tells you that eating rocks every morning will make you smarter, you could say, "That's pure hooey." You're not just saying they're a little wrong — you're saying their claim is total garbage, completely ridiculous.

This is where hooey gets interesting. It is not a cold, neutral dismissal. It carries a tone — somewhere between irritation and amusement. When someone says hooey, there's often a slight eye-roll behind it, a sense of "I can't believe anyone would actually say or believe this."

It is not the word you use for a small factual error. It is the word you reach for when something is so obviously baseless, so thoroughly made-up or foolish, that it almost insults your intelligence. A small mistake is not hooey. A conspiracy theory someone insists is true — that could absolutely be called hooey.

Hooey can describe many different kinds of nonsense:

  • False claims — "All that hooey about the medication curing everything is dangerous."
  • Silly excuses — "He gave me some hooey about the dog eating his homework."
  • Empty promises — "The politician's speech was full of hooey."
  • Baseless beliefs — "She doesn't believe in all that hooey about luck charms."
  • Exaggerated boasting — "Half of what he says about himself is hooey."

In every case, the common thread is the same: the content is not grounded in truth or reality, and the speaker finds it ridiculous or irritating.

Hooey is an informal, colloquial word — meaning you would use it in casual, everyday conversation, not in formal writing, academic papers, or professional settings. It belongs to American English specifically, and while it is understood widely, it has a slightly old-fashioned or folksy flavor, like something a grandparent might say. That said, people still use it today, often for humorous effect or to sound charmingly exasperated.

You would never say hooey in a courtroom, a business report, or a medical journal. But around the dinner table, in a casual argument, or in a lighthearted article? Perfectly at home.

You may have heard words like nonsense, rubbish, baloney, hogwash, malarkey, bunk, or drivel. Hooey belongs to exactly this family. They all mean roughly the same thing — something false and foolish — but each has its own personality. Hooey leans toward being playful and folksy, a little softer and more amused than, say, "rubbish" (which can sound more British and sharp) or "drivel" (which sounds more intellectual and contemptuous). If someone says "That's drivel," it sounds sophisticated. If someone says "That's hooey," it sounds like they're shaking their head with a smirk.

What it meansNonsense; something completely false, foolish, or baseless
ToneDismissive, mildly exasperated, often a little amused
StrengthStrong dismissal — not just "slightly wrong" but "totally ridiculous"

If you can replace a word or phrase with "total nonsense that nobody should believe" and the sentence still means the same thing — that's hooey.
